title: Harlem rent parties and Buffet Flats
summary: He says he was above rent parties and describes Buffet Flats with pianolas, liquor in teapots and rooms upstairs, and landlords favouring madams.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: I see. Before we get to that, let me just ask you about Harlem in those days. Did you play rent parties there like you had in --
No, I didn't have no need. I was working steady now, above that.
So you're above the rent parties.
Yeah. There were rent parties going on, but they were for youngsters. I called myself a finished musician, now.
What about Buffet Flats.
Well, we'd go up there and drink.
What were the Buffet Flats like?
Well, the Buffet Flats, at this time, they began to have pianolas.
Uh hunh.

And they didn't have any piano players, but they had the pianolas. Put a Lucky Roberts piano roll on, Peter Wedling. And some of the other fellows that had made rolls for the piano roll companies. And then you set there and drink. Because it was prohibition. And they would serve you the liquor in a pitcher and a cup, like you was having tea. And you'd sit there and drink and you'd meet a little lady friend and all like that, see. And they had at the Buffet Flat, it was more like a
motel. They had rooms for you if you got that far.
Yes, well, I've heard that all kinds of things went on there. Everything imaginable that was illegal went on there in the Buffet Flats.
Absolutely, that's what I'm saying. It was like a motel. If you'd get that far. Depending on who your friend was, you could do anything you wanted to. The sky was your limit.
I see.

And they had to make money, that's because the rent would go up for the other people. Because the woman that -- say, this apartment, there's six apartments in this house. Well, the poor people can't afford it there, with $30, $35 a month.
Uh hunh.
But the madam that was running the Buffet Flats, she was supposed to pay $75.00 or $100.00 a month, because she was making that some times in one night.
Right.

You see, so when the real estate agent would say, "Look here, I'm -- I can make enough if I can get a couple of buffet flats in here, I can make more than I'm making on these other people." And so, he'd be ready to dispossess those people if they got anyways back in their rent. And give it to somebody running an illegitimate house, you see?
I see.
The house of flowers, or whatever you want to call it.

You know, see, so that's what went on. But the Buffet Flats were very popular because you couldn't very well do what you wanted in the cabaret, you know. Because, see, most of the people around that time was married or had a girl friend, and if you had a stranger, it would be back even before you could get back home -- somebody'd been there ahead of you and told the people at home, "I just saw your husband, your boyfriend, around the corner with Anna Jones." And it'd be one of those things like Frankie and Johnny, you know.
Right. But did -- why were they called Buffet Flats. Do you know?
Well, Buffet Flats -- the only thing I know, it would come from like you see in a lot of railroads -- porters, like --
Right.
Because they'd be running, have a run from here to Chicago, or Chicago to here, why they'd stop in -- why, they worked in the buffet cars on the train, I think it got --
I've heard that before, you're really just confirming that.
Yes. Well, they'd call it a buffet flat.
Why, because they used to, they were used to that, and that was the biggest trade.
And porters had a high standing, didn't they?
Oh, yeah.
Because they were a good catch.

They were a very good catch, you know, in that time. The girls would go for them. And they didn't stay there either. So they didn't tie them right down. One of the fellows stayin' there all the time, he was doin' them like that, see?
(laugh)
But he thought he wouldn't be back for a -- another seven or eight days on his next run. And they had the freedom.
